stage1_evidence_shown.label: BACKGROUND
stage1_evidence_shown.context: Tinnitus can be related to many different aetiologies such as hearing loss or a noise trauma, but it can also be related to the somatosensory system of the cervical spine, called cervicogenic somatic tinnitus (CST). Case studies suggest a positive effect of cervical spine treatment on tinnitus complaints in patients with CST, but no experimental studies are available.

stage1_evidence_shown.label: OBJECTIVE
stage1_evidence_shown.context: To investigate the effect of a multimodal cervical physical therapy treatment on tinnitus complaints in patients with CST.

stage1_evidence_shown.label: PATIENTS
stage1_evidence_shown.context: Patients with a combination of severe subjective tinnitus (Tinnitus Functional Index (TFI): 25-90 points) and neck complaints (Neck Bournemouth Questionnaire (NBQ) > 14 points).

stage1_evidence_shown.label: INTERVENTION
stage1_evidence_shown.context: All patients received cervical physical therapy for 6 weeks (12 sessions). Patients were randomized in an immediate-start therapy group (n = 19) and a 6-week delayed-start therapy group (n = 19).

stage1_evidence_shown.label: MEASUREMENTS
stage1_evidence_shown.context: TFI and NBQ-scores were documented at baseline, after the wait-and-see period in the delayed-start group, after treatment and after 6 weeks follow-up. The Global Perceived Effect (GPE) was documented at all measuring moments, except at baseline.

stage2_added_evidence.label: RESULTS
stage2_added_evidence.context: In all patients (n = 38) TFI and NBQ-scores decreased significantly after treatment (p = 0.04 and p < 0.001). NBQ-scores remained significantly lower after follow-up (p = 0.001). Immediately after treatment, 53% (n = 38) experienced substantial improvement of tinnitus. This effect was maintained in 24% of patients after follow-up at six weeks.
